title: What Guardog Does
description: Guardog is a local package security scanner for npm and PyPI. It checks packages against CVE databases, reputation signals, code pattern analysis, and optional VirusTotal lookups before you install or commit dependencies. Every scan ends with one of three verdicts: SILENT (safe), WHINE (suspicious), or BARK (dangerous). Start here to understand what problem Guardog solves and what signals it uses.

title: CLI Entry Point
description: src/index.js is where all user-facing commands land. It exports the GuardDog class and wires up three subcommands: analyze (single package), batch (list from JSON), and doctor (system health). It also handles setup, git-hook management, and nightly-scan scheduling. Reading this file gives you the full map of what Guardog can do from the terminal.

title: Verdict Scoring Thresholds
description: All scanner results collapse into a single numeric score. config/config.json defines the cutoffs: BARK at 100 or above (danger, Telegram alert sent), WHINE between 50 and 99 (suspicious, warn user), and SILENT below 50 (safe). The CLAUDE.md skill doc captures these thresholds in compact form. Understanding the scoring system before reading individual scanners makes the weights make sense.

title: CVE Database Lookup
description: src/cve-checker.js queries the OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities) database for known CVEs affecting a package and version. It returns a list of advisories with severity levels that the decision tree converts into a threat score. This is the most straightforward scanner: a package name and ecosystem go in, a list of published vulnerabilities comes out.

title: Reputation Signals
description: src/reputation-checker.js fetches package metadata from npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and GitHub to build a reputation profile. Signals include download counts, maintainer count, time since last publish, whether a source repo exists, and open security issues. config/trusted-providers.json contains an allowlist of publishers whose packages skip detailed scanning to reduce false positives.

title: Suspicious Code Patterns
description: src/pattern-analyzer.js downloads the package tarball and scans its source files with a set of regex patterns that flag common malware techniques: base64 obfuscation, process spawning, network exfiltration calls, and credential harvesting. Each matched pattern contributes to the score with a configurable weight. This is the only scanner that actually reads package code rather than relying on external metadata.

title: Threat Intelligence Aggregation
description: src/threat-intel.js aggregates advisory data from OSV, GitHub Advisories, NVD (National Vulnerability Database), and CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog). Results are cached to disk to avoid redundant network calls. This scanner goes broader than cve-checker: it cross-references multiple authoritative threat feeds and flags packages with active exploitation evidence.

title: VirusTotal Integration
description: src/virustotal-scanner.js submits the package download URL or file hash to the VirusTotal v3 API and parses how many antivirus engines flagged it. This check is optional and requires an API key in .env. When a VirusTotal hit is returned, it carries heavy weight in the decision tree because multi-engine detection is a strong malware signal.

title: Decision Tree Verdict
description: src/decision-tree.js receives all scanner outputs and combines them into a total threat score using configurable weights. It first checks whether the publisher is on the trusted-providers allowlist and short-circuits if so. Otherwise it sums the CVE score, reputation score, pattern score, threat-intel score, and VirusTotal score, then maps the total to BARK, WHINE, or SILENT along with a reasons array explaining what drove the verdict.

title: Operator Alerts
description: src/telegram-alert.js formats and delivers a Telegram bot message whenever a scan verdict reaches BARK level. The message includes the package name, ecosystem, total threat score, and the list of reasons from the decision tree. This is the human-in-the-loop output: everything upstream is automated, and Telegram is where a dangerous finding surfaces to the operator.

title: Developer Workflow Hooks
description: bin/git-precommit-hook.sh blocks a git commit when staged package.json changes contain a package that returns BARK. bin/npm-postinstall-hook.sh runs an automatic scan after every npm install. These two scripts embed Guardog into the normal development workflow so dangerous packages are caught at the moment of introduction, without requiring the developer to remember to run a manual scan.

title: Scheduled Automation
description: bin/cron-nightly-scan.sh runs at 2:30 AM (GMT+8) and invokes bin/nightly-scan.js, which walks the filesystem to discover all package.json files and scans their dependencies. bin/threat-intel-scan.sh runs the threat intelligence refresh at 3:00 AM. Together these scripts keep threat data current and catch supply-chain attacks on packages that were safe when first installed.

title: Setup and Path Resolution
description: src/setup.js is the interactive setup wizard invoked by guardog setup. It persists user configuration, installs or removes the git pre-commit hook, and schedules or removes the nightly cron job. src/paths.js provides a single place where the tool resolves its home directory, data directory, config path, and .env path, making the rest of the codebase location-independent.
